paragraphs: ARROW addresses the computational expense of discovering causal relationships in time series. The paper identifies three sources of inefficiency: organizing observations into bins, choosing appropriate time lags, and searching through large sets of possible explanatory variables. Its contribution is an accelerator that can be applied to existing discovery algorithms.

The method combines three components. Time Weaving encodes time series to capture their changing trends while reducing computational complexity. A lag discovery strategy uses XOR operations, together with a theorem for obtaining the optimal lag. A pruning strategy then narrows the candidate variables to those judged most relevant, reducing the search required to identify causal relationships.

The authors apply ARROW to four types of causal discovery algorithms and evaluate it on 25 synthetic and real-world datasets. They report speedups reaching 153 times those of the original algorithms, with higher accuracy in most cases. These results support the usefulness of improving data encoding, lag selection, and candidate search together; the maximum speedup is a reported outcome, rather than a uniform gain across every case.
icml-2025-arrow-accelerator-for-time-ser.tldr: ARROW accelerates time series causal discovery through efficient encoding, lag selection, and candidate pruning, reaching 153-fold speedups in the reported evaluations.

paragraphs: Multi-view clustering combines different sources of information to group related examples. This can work well when the views are clean, but noisy information can undermine the representations used for clustering. AIRMVC tackles this problem by making noise identification and correction explicit parts of the learning process.

The framework treats noisy data identification as anomaly identification using a Gaussian mixture model. The resulting judgments guide a hybrid rectification strategy intended to reduce the damage caused by noise. A noise-robust contrastive mechanism then learns representations from the corrected information. These components connect the detection of problematic data with changes to how representations are learned.

The paper also provides a theoretical proof that the learned representations can discard noisy information, supporting their usefulness for downstream tasks. Experiments on six benchmark datasets show stronger robustness than the compared state-of-the-art algorithms in noisy scenarios. The stated contribution therefore combines a practical pipeline with theoretical support: identify unreliable information, mitigate its effects, and learn representations that better preserve useful structure for clustering.
icml-2025-automatically-identify-and-rec.tldr: AIRMVC identifies and rectifies noisy multi-view data before learning contrastive representations, improving clustering robustness in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: Long chains of thought give language models room to backtrack, correct mistakes, and develop structured solutions. This paper investigates the training conditions that help such extended reasoning emerge. It studies supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning to clarify which choices make training more efficient and which help sustain the growth of reasoning trajectories.

The experiments find that supervised fine-tuning is helpful without being strictly required: it simplifies training and improves efficiency. Increasing training compute tends to produce reasoning capabilities, but does not guarantee them. The authors identify reward shaping as essential for stabilizing the growth of chain-of-thought length, showing that additional compute and a suitable training signal play different roles.

A further finding concerns the availability of verifiable rewards. Scaling these signals is critical for reinforcement learning, and filtered solutions extracted from the web show promising potential despite containing noise. This is particularly relevant to reasoning outside the training distribution, including STEM problems. The study offers practical training guidance while preserving an important distinction: longer training can encourage reasoning, but its emergence remains contingent on the training setup.
icml-2025-demystifying-long-chain-of-tho.tldr: Experiments clarify how supervised fine-tuning, reward shaping, and scalable verifiable rewards help develop long reasoning chains without guaranteeing their emergence.

paragraphs: Adaptive subgradient methods can use compressed matrix summaries to reduce the burden of optimization. This paper studies summaries produced by Frequent Directions, a matrix sketching technique. Existing guarantees have two drawbacks: regret bounds grow linearly with dimension, and each round costs O(τ²d), where τ is the sketch size and d is the dimension.

The proposed FTSL algorithm combines Frequent Directions with a primal-dual formulation and adds back accumulated information discarded during sketching. Its regret bound is independent of dimension. Using a faster version of Frequent Directions reduces the per-round cost to O(τd) while preserving that bound. The distinction matters: the guarantee becomes dimension-free, although the computation still depends on d.

The authors also adapt Frequent Directions to Shampoo for optimization involving matrix variables, including neural network training. Their primal-dual analysis yields an improved dimension-free regret bound for this structured setting. Experiments support the efficiency and effectiveness of the approaches. Together, the contributions address both the quality of theoretical guarantees and the practical expense of maintaining useful gradient information.
icml-2025-dimension-free-adaptive-subgra.tldr: New Frequent Directions optimization methods obtain dimension-free regret bounds while reducing sketching costs and extending the approach to Shampoo.

paragraphs: Offline model-based optimization uses an existing dataset to propose designs expected to receive high rewards. The paper argues that candidate quality is only part of the goal: the final set should also contain varied optimal and near-optimal configurations. A collection of strong designs is more useful for this objective when it represents multiple possibilities.

DynAMO makes diversity an explicit optimization objective by expressing it as distribution matching. The distribution of proposed designs is encouraged to capture the diversity already present in the offline dataset. This gives diversity a concrete reference and connects the desired variety of the final candidates to information available before optimization begins.

The method is presented as a way to introduce this objective into offline model-based optimization and can be combined with common optimization methods. Across experiments spanning several scientific domains, it significantly improves candidate diversity while continuing to find high-quality designs. The findings support treating diversity as something to optimize deliberately alongside reward, with the offline dataset supplying the variety that distribution matching seeks to preserve.
icml-2025-diversity-by-design-leveraging.tldr: DynAMO uses distribution matching to increase the diversity of offline optimization candidates while retaining high design quality in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: Implicit neural representations store data in a neural representation that is compact and expressive. Using this data for vision tasks presents a trade-off: purely implicit networks can have restricted operations and performance, while converting the representation into a raster can discard useful structure. DVI connects implicit representations with existing raster-based vision networks.

Its key operation extracts semantic information from higher-order derivative maps of the implicit representation. These maps provide information about how the representation changes, which DVI fuses into a pre-existing raster-based network. The resulting architecture uses established vision methods while adding task-relevant information drawn from the structure of the implicit representation.

Experiments cover five vision tasks across three data modalities, with DVI outperforming the existing methods evaluated. The study also examines individual components, different ways of computing derivatives, and the effects of derivative order. These analyses support the value of the derivative-based design. The central finding is that implicit representations can contribute useful semantic information beyond what is retained by straightforward raster conversion.
icml-2025-dvi-a-derivative-based-vision-.tldr: DVI enriches raster-based vision networks with higher-order derivative information from implicit neural representations, improving results across the evaluated tasks.

paragraphs: Different modalities can repeat information, contribute information individually, or provide information through their combination. These interactions are described as redundancy, uniqueness, and synergy. The paper addresses the difficulty of measuring them for individual examples, where accurate estimates must also be computationally practical.

The Lightweight Sample-wise Multimodal Interaction estimator, or LSMI, is grounded in pointwise information theory. The authors first develop a framework for estimating redundancy, choosing an information measure suited to decomposing this interaction. They then build a more general interaction estimator using efficient entropy estimation designed for individual samples from continuous distributions.

Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets support LSMI’s precision and efficiency. Measuring interactions at the sample level reveals differences between individual examples and between categories that broader summaries can conceal. The paper connects these measurements to practical uses: dividing samples according to redundancy, targeting knowledge distillation, and forming model ensembles with awareness of modality interactions. Its contribution is therefore both an estimation method and a way to make fine-grained information relationships useful in multimodal systems.
icml-2025-efficient-quantification-of-mu.tldr: LSMI efficiently estimates multimodal information interactions for individual samples, supporting finer analysis and interaction-aware learning strategies.

paragraphs: Graph models can struggle when the environment changes between training and use. Existing approaches often seek causal subgraphs while treating spurious subgraphs as representations of the environment. This paper argues that such a representation is too narrow: environmental changes can involve more than the variation expressed by spurious graph structure.

NeGo expands the space used to infer environmental factors. Its negative prompt environment inference component extracts underlying environment information, drawing inspiration from prompt learning. An environment-enhanced invariant subgraph learning component then uses the inferred environment embedding to support the extraction of causal subgraphs under distribution shifts.

This connects a broader account of the environment to the graph features intended to remain useful across environments. Evaluations cover synthetic and real-world datasets across domains, with NeGo outperforming baselines on nearly all datasets. The results support the paper’s diagnosis that restricting environmental information to spurious subgraphs can hinder generalization. They also support using richer inferred environment information to improve invariant graph learning under the evaluated shifts.
icml-2025-enhancing-graph-invariant-lear.tldr: NeGo broadens environmental inference beyond spurious subgraphs to improve graph generalization under distribution shifts.

paragraphs: Loss reweighting changes how strongly different data influence a language model’s unlearning objective. Although this technique has shown benefits, the reasons particular weighting schemes work remain unclear. The paper separates two goals: saturation emphasizes data that have not been sufficiently optimized, while importance emphasizes data with greater influence on minimizing the loss.

The authors design strategies for each goal and compare their effects on established unlearning benchmarks. Saturation-based weighting improves efficacy more than importance-based weighting in these analyses, and combining them can provide further gains. The two approaches also behave differently: saturation typically gives less weight to lower-likelihood data, whereas importance-based weighting tends to give those data more.

The study further finds that the smoothness and granularity of the weight distribution substantially affect unlearning efficacy. These observations motivate SatImp, a simple method combining saturation and importance. Results across extensive datasets support its effectiveness. The contribution is an empirical account of what weighting schemes prioritize, together with a method that uses the complementary benefits identified in that analysis.
icml-2025-exploring-criteria-of-loss-rew.tldr: SatImp improves LLM unlearning by combining two empirically studied weighting goals: optimization saturation and data importance.

paragraphs: Compressing a 3D Gaussian Splatting representation must balance data size, reconstruction quality, and the time required to encode and decode it. The paper identifies deployment difficulties in approaches that embed data implicitly: they can be slow and rely on highly customized formats. HybridGS combines compact explicit representations with standardized point cloud encoding.

The framework first generates compact 3DGS data. A dual-channel sparse representation supervises the positions of the primitives and the bit depth used for their features. A conventional point cloud encoder then compresses this explicit data into standard output bitstreams. A rate control scheme provides a way to manage compression within this interpretable representation.

HybridGS includes no generation modules specifically intended to improve 3DGS quality. Even so, experiments show reconstruction performance comparable to state-of-the-art methods, alongside clearly faster encoding and decoding. The result supports the practical value of coordinating compact representation generation with an established data encoder. Here, maintaining reconstruction quality while simplifying and accelerating data handling is the central reported benefit.
icml-2025-hybridgs-high-efficiency-gauss.tldr: HybridGS combines compact explicit Gaussian representations with standard point cloud encoding for faster compression and decompression at comparable reconstruction quality.

paragraphs: Preference learning predicts choices from comparative judgments, but gathering human comparisons can be expensive. Classical estimation has an optimal worst-case error rate of Θ(d/n), tying the required sample count n to the feature dimension d. This paper asks how much that burden can fall when only a small number of features determine the reward.

Under a sparse random utility model with k nonzero reward parameters, the authors establish a sharp optimal rate of Θ((k/n) log(d/k)). This replaces the direct dependence on the full dimension with a dependence on sparsity and a logarithmic dimensional factor. The improvement rests on the stated sparse-model assumption, giving a precise account of when sparsity can help.

The paper also analyzes an estimator using ℓ1 regularization and shows that it achieves a near-optimal rate under mild assumptions on the Gram matrix. Experiments with synthetic data and LLM alignment data support the theoretical findings, reporting lower sample complexity and better prediction accuracy. The contribution links a statistical benefit to a practical estimation approach capable of exploiting it.
icml-2025-leveraging-sparsity-for-sample.tldr: Under a sparse preference model, the paper proves improved estimation rates and shows that ℓ1 regularization can approach them under stated matrix assumptions.

paragraphs: Language model neurons can encode several unrelated concepts, making their behavior difficult to interpret. MoE-X addresses this through the model’s architecture. Its motivation is that wide networks with sparse activations are more likely to capture interpretable factors, but directly training very large sparse networks can be computationally prohibitive.

The authors express a mixture-of-experts layer as an equivalent large, sparse multilayer perceptron. Because only some experts activate for an input, this provides a scalable way to increase hidden size while preserving sparsity. MoE-X further encourages sparse activity within each expert and changes routing to favor experts with the highest activation sparsity, directing computation toward salient features.

Evaluations on chess and natural language tasks show performance comparable to dense models with substantially better interpretability. The paper also reports better perplexity than GPT-2 and stronger interpretability than sparse-autoencoder-based approaches. These findings support incorporating interpretability objectives into the model’s computation itself. They connect the architectural choices about width, expert activity, and routing to the observed ability to identify more interpretable features.
icml-2025-mixture-of-experts-made-intrin.tldr: MoE-X builds sparsity into expert activations and routing to improve intrinsic interpretability while retaining competitive language-model performance.

paragraphs: Neural controllers can perform well while using certificate functions to support stability, but continual feedback updates can demand impractical communication resources on digital platforms. Neural ETC addresses this deployment problem by learning an event-triggered controller. Its scheduling objective is to minimize the number of triggering events while maintaining the desired control behavior.

The framework provides two practical algorithms. A path integral algorithm directly simulates event-triggered dynamics. A Monte Carlo algorithm builds on new theoretical results concerning a lower bound on the time between events. These approaches connect controller learning to the scheduling of updates, making communication frequency part of the control problem.

The authors also introduce a projection operation with an analytical expression that ensures theoretical stability and schedule optimality within their framework. Empirical comparisons with conventional neural controllers show substantially lower communication requirements and improved control performance when communication resources are constrained. The stated benefit is therefore a coordinated treatment of stability, scheduling, and control quality, with theoretical guarantees for the proposed construction and experimental support for its resource savings.
icml-2025-neural-event-triggered-control.tldr: Neural ETC learns stable event-triggered controllers with optimal scheduling, reducing communication and improving control in the evaluated constrained settings.

paragraphs: A diffusion bridge is a diffusion process constrained by conditioning information. Simulating these processes can be expensive, particularly when the required events are rare or the relevant distribution has multiple modes. This paper proposes learning the bridge dynamics with a neural network for diffusion processes in Euclidean spaces.

The method constructs a flexible variational family that approximates the probability distribution over entire bridge paths. A neural network specifies part of this family and is trained to approximate the conditioned dynamics. This formulation removes the need for computationally intensive Markov Chain Monte Carlo sampling or a model of the reverse process.

Once training is complete, the approach produces independent samples at a cost comparable to simulating the unconditioned forward process. The authors report greater robustness than existing methods across diffusion specifications and conditioning scenarios, particularly for rare events and multimodal distributions. The important efficiency claim concerns sampling after training: learning a reusable approximation makes conditioned path generation substantially more direct, while retaining flexibility across the types of processes and conditions studied.
icml-2025-neural-guided-diffusion-bridge.tldr: A neural approximation of diffusion-bridge dynamics enables efficient independent sampling after training, including challenging rare-event and multimodal settings.

paragraphs: Langevin Monte Carlo generates samples by discretizing a stochastic process. This paper analyzes its finite-computation error for non-convex targets using the Wasserstein-2 distance between distributions. Under certain log-smooth conditions and a log-Sobolev inequality, it proves an O(√d h) error bound, where d is dimension and h is the step size.

The bound yields a mixing-time guarantee of Õ(√d/ε) for accuracy ε. It matches the best stated result for strongly log-concave targets while improving known non-convex rates. The assumptions matter: the result extends beyond strong log-concavity through a different set of regularity and distributional conditions.

The proof develops a framework that controls discretization error uniformly over time. It combines finite-time mean-square convergence, uniform moment bounds, and exponential ergodicity of the underlying stochastic dynamics. The framework also handles potentials whose gradients grow superlinearly and are not globally Lipschitz, with modified samplers and associated error bounds. Numerical experiments corroborate the analysis. Together, these results extend rigorous sampling guarantees to a broader set of non-convex problems.
icml-2025-non-asymptotic-error-bounds-in.tldr: Under stated regularity and log-Sobolev assumptions, Langevin Monte Carlo achieves O(√d h) Wasserstein-2 error beyond strongly log-concave targets.

paragraphs: Occluded image contrastive learning, or OCL, is a visual pre-training approach built around randomly hiding image patches. These masks produce different views of each image, which are contrasted within a mini-batch. The goal is to learn high-level visual concepts through differences in visible content.

The design has two motivations. First, masking has the potential to reduce repeated conceptual information and expose fine-grained semantic differences between views. Second, contrastive learning can extract high-level features without the high-frequency interference and additional computational cost associated with reconstructing images. OCL therefore learns its representations without relying on hand-crafted data augmentations or extra auxiliary modules.

The paper reports that this simple approach scales well with Vision Transformers. In its stated example, a ViT-L/16 completes pre-training in 133 hours on four A100 GPUs and achieves 85.8% accuracy after downstream fine-tuning. This result supports the practicality of the proposed pre-training design at that scale. The contribution is a direct connection between patch occlusion, semantically varied views, and efficient contrastive representation learning.
icml-2025-one-leaf-reveals-the-season-oc.tldr: OCL uses randomly masked image views for efficient contrastive pre-training, learning semantic representations without hand-crafted augmentations or auxiliary modules.

paragraphs: FedLMG addresses a practical burden in diffusion-based one-shot federated learning: requiring foundation models on client devices raises their computational needs and complicates support for different client models. Its clients only train and upload local models. These models become the means of transferring client knowledge to a diffusion model held on the server.

Classification and batch normalization losses capture broad category information and detailed contextual features of client distributions. On the server, backpropagation through the uploaded models guides the diffusion model to generate synthetic data consistent with those distributions. The server then trains the aggregated model on this synthetic dataset, connecting locally learned knowledge to a shared training resource.

The paper combines theoretical analysis with quantitative and visual experiments on three large-scale real-world datasets. It reports synthetic data comparable to client data in quality and diversity, and an aggregated model exceeding every compared method and the study’s stated performance ceiling. These findings support local models as an effective knowledge-transfer medium while reducing client computation and accommodating heterogeneous clients.
icml-2025-one-shot-heterogeneous-federat.tldr: FedLMG uses uploaded local models to guide server-side diffusion, enabling heterogeneous one-shot federated learning without foundation models on clients.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning often involves competing goals, such as speed and safety. Existing multi-objective methods can cover only a limited range of desirable trade-offs and offer imprecise control over which trade-off a user receives. Preference Controllable RL, or PCRL, trains a meta-policy that accepts user preferences as input.

The intended behavior is to generate trajectories within the requested preference region of the Pareto frontier, the set of trade-offs where improving one objective requires sacrificing another. PCRL supports advanced multi-objective optimization algorithms, and the authors introduce a preference-regularized algorithm specifically for this framework. Their theoretical analysis addresses convergence and preference controllability.

Experiments compare PCRL using different optimization algorithms against state-of-the-art multi-objective RL baselines in environments with as many as six objectives. The proposed method shows substantially better controllability and produces Pareto solutions with better diversity and utilities. These findings support learning a policy whose behavior can be adjusted through preferences, while also improving the range and quality of available trade-offs in the evaluated settings.
icml-2025-preference-controllable-reinfo.tldr: PCRL trains preference-conditioned policies that provide more precise control over competing objectives and better trade-off diversity in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: Safe offline reinforcement learning aims to learn useful policies from existing data without risky online interaction. A challenge appears when testing presents unfamiliar combinations of reward-related and cost-related state information. SDQC addresses this by separating global observations into representations associated with reward and cost.

The framework uses Q-supervised contrastive representation learning to perform this separation. The authors theoretically show that their method produces a coarser representation while preserving the optimal policy, compared with classical representation approaches that typically require model-based estimation. This supports generalization by allowing a less detailed state representation to retain the distinctions needed for optimal decisions.

On DSRL benchmark problems, SDQC outperforms the compared algorithms and achieves almost zero violations on more than half the tasks. The cited state-of-the-art algorithm reaches that level on a quarter of the tasks. Further experiments demonstrate stronger generalization to unseen environments. These results support state decoupling as a useful approach to unfamiliar observations, while the reported near-zero violations remain empirical outcomes rather than a claim of universal safety.
icml-2025-q-supervised-contrastive-repre.tldr: SDQC separates reward and cost representations to improve safe offline RL generalization, achieving almost zero violations on more than half the evaluated DSRL tasks.

paragraphs: Retrieval-augmented generation can help vision-language models answer visual questions by supplying external knowledge. Yet retrieved material may lack useful reasoning examples, and the resulting responses can be inconsistent. RCTS addresses both the content of the knowledge base and the selection of examples provided to the model.

The framework first enriches its knowledge base with reasoning patterns through a self-consistent evaluation mechanism. It then uses Monte Carlo Tree Search with heuristic rewards to re-rank examples and prioritize those most relevant to the question. These steps connect the availability of reasoning-rich material with a search procedure for choosing useful context.

Experiments on multiple visual question answering datasets report state-of-the-art performance and substantial improvements over in-context learning and vanilla retrieval-augmented generation. The results support the combined value of the enriched knowledge base and the re-ranking method. The broader significance is that retrieval quality depends on more than having related information available: in this framework, reasoning examples and their ordering help produce better and more consistent answers.
icml-2025-re-ranking-reasoning-context-w.tldr: RCTS improves visual question answering by enriching retrieved knowledge with reasoning examples and re-ranking them through heuristic-guided tree search.

paragraphs: This paper examines what training signal makes a useful DNA representation. The authors argue that unsupervised learning from sequence alone is insufficient because genomic profiles, including chromatin accessibility, regulate DNA function. They investigate supervised prediction of those profiles as a more effective basis for learning transferable representations.

SPACE, short for Species-Profile Adaptive Collaborative Experts, uses a mixture-of-experts architecture to address the multiple species and profiles involved in this prediction task. Its experts help capture relationships between sequences across those species and genomic profiles. This connects the representation-learning objective to biological information that sequence-only pre-training does not directly provide.

Extensive experiments across various tasks yield state-of-the-art performance for the proposed model. The results support the claim that a supervised genomic profile predictor can also serve as a powerful DNA representation learner. The paper’s contribution combines this training argument with an architecture suited to the structure of the supervision: multiple profiles and species become part of how the model learns useful relationships in DNA.
icml-2025-space-your-genomic-profile-pre.tldr: SPACE uses supervised genomic profile prediction and collaborative experts across species and profiles to learn strong DNA representations.

paragraphs: Out-of-distribution detection seeks to reject inputs that fall outside a model’s training distribution. Memorizing atypical training examples late in training can hurt this ability, but directly forgetting those examples can also damage generalization on familiar data. Progressive Self-Knowledge Distillation, or PSKD, addresses this tension by transferring uncertainty information from the model’s own training history.

PSKD adaptively chooses a historical version of the model as a teacher using pseudo-outliers. It then distills uncertainty-related knowledge at multiple levels, including features and output responses. The teacher supplies targets that carry uncertainty information, allowing the current model to learn more than the final predictions alone.

The paper reports improved in-distribution generalization and uncertainty estimation for detecting unfamiliar inputs. Experiments across multiple out-of-distribution scenarios support the framework’s effectiveness and broad applicability. PSKD is also described as compatible with most existing methods and usable as a plugin. Its contribution is a training strategy that uses earlier model knowledge to improve rejection decisions while preserving stronger performance on familiar data.
icml-2025-strengthen-out-of-distribution.tldr: PSKD distills uncertainty from a model’s training history to improve out-of-distribution detection and in-distribution generalization.

paragraphs: Unsupervised multi-object segmentation aims to identify separate objects in a single image without human labels. Existing approaches often learn through image reconstruction or group pixels using pretrained features, but can struggle with complex real-world objects and crowded scenes. unMORE introduces a two-stage pipeline designed to discover many such objects.

The first stage explicitly learns three levels of object-centric representations. These learned representations provide object priors for a second-stage multi-object reasoning module. That reasoning module is network-free and requires no human labels. The design therefore separates learning useful object information from the subsequent reasoning that identifies multiple objects in an image.

Experiments across six real-world benchmark datasets, including COCO, show substantial improvements over the existing unsupervised methods evaluated. The paper particularly highlights crowded images, where unMORE succeeds while the compared baselines collapse. These findings support the value of explicitly learned object-centric representations combined with a separate reasoning stage. The network-free claim applies to the reasoning module, while representation learning remains part of the overall pipeline.
icml-2025-unmore-unsupervised-multi-obje.tldr: unMORE combines learned object-centric representations with network-free reasoning to improve unsupervised segmentation of complex and crowded real-world images.

paragraphs: Customized latent diffusion models can learn from only a few images, creating privacy concerns when used to generate fake depictions. This paper studies adversarial attacks intended to prevent generated images from preserving identity. It identifies variance in the variational autoencoder’s latent code as a key factor: larger variance produces stronger distortion and can ultimately erase semantic information.

The authors propose a Laplace-based loss that follows the fastest local direction of variance growth, making each optimization step locally optimal. Their analysis finds that existing losses can misalign gradient signs with variance growth and optimize inefficiently across variance distributions. A second, Lagrange Entropy-based loss is introduced to address these problems.

Experiments on CelebA-HQ and VGGFace2 report state-of-the-art performance. Both losses cause the evaluated diffusion models to generate pure-noise images with identity semantics completely erased. The methods also show strong transfer across different models and low computational requirements. These results connect a specific property of latent representations to more effective semantic erasure, supporting the proposed methods as a practical privacy-protection approach.
icml-2025-variance-as-a-catalyst-efficie.tldr: Two variance-focused adversarial losses erase identity semantics in the evaluated customized diffusion models while offering efficient optimization and strong transferability.

paragraphs: Dynamic data selection speeds training by using fewer examples, but the resulting loss of diversity can harm generalization. Data augmentation can increase diversity, yet selecting samples and augmenting them independently may miss useful interactions. This paper introduces an online training framework that makes these decisions together.

For each sample, the method estimates a joint distribution involving local density and multimodal semantic consistency. It uses this information to select examples suited to augmentation while limiting noisy or ambiguous data. Selection is therefore guided partly by how useful the retained examples will be when augmented, enabling a greater reduction in dataset size without sacrificing generalization in the reported evaluations.

Experiments across benchmark datasets and architectures show improvements over existing state-of-the-art approaches. One reported result reduces ImageNet-1k training costs by 50% without performance loss. The method also improves noise resistance and model robustness. These findings support coordinating selection with augmentation as a practical route to faster training, with the gains arising from the quality and diversity of the chosen training data.
icml-2025-when-dynamic-data-selection-me.tldr: Jointly choosing training samples and their suitability for augmentation reduces training costs while preserving performance and improving robustness in the reported experiments.
